title: TB9-01665
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): He appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (a.k.a. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX) (the Appellant) is citizen of Nigeria. In his Notice of Appeal he writes his surname as XXXX XXXX XXXX but on his Nigerian identity documents and in his Basis of Claim (BOC) form his surname is written as XXXX XXXX XXXX.1 He alleges a fear of returning to Nigeria based on his political opinion. He appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection. The RPD found that the Appellant is not credible. The Appellant argues that this finding is in error. I disagree. Having independently assessed all of the evidence, including the RPD hearing audio-recording, I find that the RPD did not err and that the Appellant's claim is not credible.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. BACKGROUND The Appellant's allegations

The Appellant alleges in his BOC form that he is a "XXXX XXXX XXXX" of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).2 He further alleges that he runs an XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in Oyo state for young school leavers and the unemployed. The Appellant alleges that he owns XXXX in Oyo state and that a group of Fulani herdsmen have attacked his XXXX on multiple occasions. He alleges that the attacks were politically motivated. Specifically, he alleges that the herdsmen attacked his land on April 20, 2016, assaulting and injuring his XXXX manager. He alleges that his XXXX was attacked again on September 1, 2017, when the herdsmen advised the XXXX manager that the Appellant must abandon the PDP and join the rival All Progressives Congress (APC). The Appellant alleges that he was summoned to a meeting with the APC Chairman in Oyo state on September 18, 2017. Despite having a valid US visitor visa at this time, the Appellant alleges that he attended this meeting with his agent of persecution. He alleges that during this meeting he was given two weeks to join the APC. He remained in Nigeria after this deadline passed. On XXXX XXXX, 2017, the Appellant left Nigeria for the United States (US) and entered Canada irregularly on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, where he initiated his claim. He alleges that his spouse and children remain living in Nigeria, having relocated to neighbouring Ogun State. The RPD's Decision

The RPD found the Appellant and his allegations not credible for the following reasons: * The Appellant omitted from his BOC several threatening telephone calls that he alleges he received in September 2017 and October 2017 which convinced him to flee Nigeria; * The Appellant's testimony about why he obtained a US visa in July 2017 and when he decided to leave Nigeria was confusing and evolving; and * Despite the Appellant's allegation that his XXXX was invaded on April 20, 2016 and September 1, 2017, the PDP letter states that the farm was invaded on May 30, 2016.

The Appellant's claim was rejected on December 19, 2018. On appeal, the Appellant provides the following proposed new evidence: a. PDP letter, dated February 8, 2019; b. Two newspaper articles, dated between February 2019 and March 2019; and c. Independent National Electoral Commission March 9, 2019 general elections, list of governors and deputy governors elect.3

According to subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA),4 I can only accept evidence that: i. Arose after the RPD decision; or ii. Was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. Could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have been presented to the RPD before the decision.

If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.5 According to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA,6 I may only hold an oral hearing where the accepted new evidence: i. Raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal; and ii. Is central to the decision of the claim; and iii. If accepted, justifies allowing or rejecting the claim.
If the new evidence meets each requirement I must decide whether to hold a hearing.
I find that the evidence in item (a) is inadmissible and the evidence in items (b) and (c) is admissible but does not require an oral hearing. The PDP letter described in item (a) is inadmissible

The PDP letter is dated February 8, 2019. It attempts to correct an earlier PDP letter before the RPD, dated May 30, 2016. Despite the Appellant's allegation that his XXXX was invaded on April 20, 2016, the 2016 PDP letter states that the Appellant's XXXX was invaded on May 30, 2016.7 The Appellant was asked about this discrepancy at the RPD hearing and explained that this must be an error.8 The February 8, 2019 PDP letter in item (a) states that the farm attack was on "20th April 2016 not 30th May 2016 as erroneously stated."9

In considering whether the February 2019 PDP letter in item (a) arose after the rejection of the claim, on December 19, 2018, I will not restrict my analysis to the date of the letter. A document's newness cannot be tested solely by the date of its creation; what is important is the event sought to be proven by the evidence.10 Old evidence remains old evidence, even if it is placed in a new document with a recent date.11 Where proposed new evidence is "not new or newly discovered, merely revised" the Appellant must provide a reasonable explanation for why the evidence was not provided to the RPD prior to the rejection of the claim.12

Counsel argues that item (a) is admissible under 110(4) because it was "unobtainable despite the Appellant's diligent efforts."13 According to the Appellant's sworn statement: After my hearing before the RPD on December 19, 2019 I contacted the executive members of the PDP, Oyo State and brought to their attention the mistake on their letter dated 30th May 2016 stating that my XXXX was attacked on the same day. They promised to review their file and get back to me, but warned that they would not be to do so immediately since they were enthralled in electioneering campaigns for the February/March 2019 elections [emphasis added].14

Contrary to the Appellant's sworn statement, his RPD hearing took place on November 2, 2018, not December 19, 2019. Indeed, December 19, 2019 post-dates the Appellant's sworn statement on appeal to the RAD, dated March 22, 2019. However, even if the Appellant meant to write 2018 instead of 2019, this is the date of the RPD decision, not the RPD hearing. He has not explained whether he made any efforts to obtain this letter in the one-and-a-half months between his November 2, 2018 RPD hearing and December 19, 2018 RPD decision. In accordance with the Federal Court decision in Nteta-Tshamala, I find the Appellant's explanation inadequate.15

The new evidence provisions are not the Appellant's opportunity to complete a deficient record submitted to the RPD.16 Claimants must put their best foot forward before the RPD.17 I do not find that item (a) arose after the RPD decision, or was not reasonably available at the time of the decision, or could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have been presented to the RPD before the decision. Item (a) is inadmissible. The evidence described in items (b) and (c) is admissible but does not require a hearing

The two newspaper articles in item (b) and the list of governors and deputy governors elect in item (c) address the March 2019 election results in Oyo state. Both items post-date the RPD rejection and are therefore admissible under 110(4). The evidence is prima facie credible as it is from newspaper reports as well as the Nigerian Independent National Electoral Commission. It is relevant to the claim in so far as it provides information about the current political climate and indicates that PDP candidates were elected in Oyo State in March 2019. It is new in that it provides information that was not before the RPD. I admit items (b) and (c) into evidence. However, I find that they do not meet the requirements for a hearing as they do not justify allowing or rejecting the claim. Notice regarding any document or written submissions in light of the COVID-19 pandemic

On June 15, 2020, the Board provided Counsel with a notice related to the COVID-19 pandemic. This notice advised Counsel that he has 30 days from the date that he receives this notice to submit any document or written submission in support of the appeal. He was also advised that any document or written submissions in support of the appeal will be accepted without an application and that the other requirements of Rule 29 and 110(4) continue to apply. Counsel has not submitted any document or written submissions in response to this notice.

I am reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of correctness as I do not find the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage. I have conducted an independent assessment of the evidence to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred.18 In conducting my independent assessment of the evidence I am mindful that the responsibility rests with the Appellant to raise any potential grounds of appeal that arise from the RPD decision.19 Issues on appeal

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred, as follows: * In making microscopic credibility findings on peripheral issues, including his omission of threatening telephone calls from the BOC and his delay in fleeing Nigeria; and * In failing to assess the other credible evidence submitted in support of his claim and failing to take into consideration his PDP party profile.

In assessing whether there are valid reasons to doubt the Appellant's credibility, I am mindful of the difficulties in establishing a claim, including nervousness in the hearing room. I have also taken into consideration the Appellant's completion of a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.20 He read and understood his BOC in English and testified before the RPD in English. No medical evidence was provided regarding any cognitive and/or memory impairments. After listening to the entire RPD hearing audio-recording and independently assessing all of the evidence on a cumulative basis, I find that material credibility concerns were not reasonably explained and that the presumption of truthfulness has been rebutted. I find that the RPD was correct in its determination that the Appellant is not credible. The Appellant's omission of threatening calls is material and undermines his credibility

The Appellant alleged in testimony that he received "several threat calls" between September 19, 2017 and the first week of XXXX 2017.21 He alleged that these calls were anonymous, that the callers warned him that they would kill him, and that the threat was real.22 He further alleged that he decided to leave Nigeria during the first week of XXXX 2017 when he continued to receive these threatening calls.23 However, none of these alleged telephone threats were included in the BOC.24 The Appellant explained that he omitted these multiple threatening telephone calls from his BOC because he was confused and afraid for his life.25 The RPD did not accept this explanation as reasonable, noting that these calls are material as they precipitated his decision to flee Nigeria.26 Counsel argues that the RPD was microscopic and drew an adverse inference based on a peripheral issue. Having independently assessed the evidence, I am not persuaded by Counsel's arguments. I find that the RPD did not err and that the Appellant's omission of these threatening telephone calls from his BOC is material and undermines his credibility.

As the RPD correctly notes, the Appellant was represented by Counsel during the preparation of his BOC through to his RPD hearing. The Appellant failed to include these alleged telephone threats despite the clear instructions in the BOC that a Claimant is to include everything that is important for their claim. I note that the Appellant has an MBA and fluently speaks English, having signed his BOC in English and testified in English before the RPD. Even when he was asked at the beginning of his RPD hearing, the Appellant confirmed under solemn affirmation that his BOC is complete, true, and correct. No amendments were provided.

I appreciate that refugee hearings are stressful and that recalling incidents that occurred in the past may be difficult. However, I do not accept the Appellant's explanation that his confusion and fear led him to omit the very death threats that convinced him to flee Nigeria. This is not a minor or peripheral detail and this omission goes to the heart of his allegation that he is at risk from political opponents in Nigeria, the core of his claim. It is not the case that the Appellant simply forgot to mention a detail in his testimony that he had included in his BOC. Rather, he omitted from his narrative multiple telephone calls in which his life was directly threatened. These are the very calls that he alleges convinced him that he could no longer remain in Nigeria.

Having independently assessed the evidence, I find that the RPD did not err. I find that this omission is material and significantly undermines the Appellant's credibility. The Appellant's evolving testimony and delay in leaving undermine his credibility

The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony about the purpose of his US visa, when he decided to flee Nigeria, and the reason for his three-month delay in leaving after his US visa was issued, was evolving and undermined his credibility. Counsel argues that the RPD was microscopic and improperly drew an adverse inference based on a peripheral issue. I do not find Counsel's arguments persuasive. I find that the RPD did not err and that the Appellant's evolving testimony and delay in fleeing Nigeria undermine his credibility.

Having listened to the audio-recording of the RPD hearing, I note that there were several key instances when the Appellant's statements were evolving and contradictory. The Appellant's US visitor visa was issued on July 17, 2017.27 When the RPD asked the Appellant the purpose of obtaining the US visa, he responded that he obtained the visa to escape Nigeria to save his life.28 However, as discussed earlier in my Reasons, the Appellant also alleged that it was only in October 2017, after he received the alleged threatening telephone calls, that he decided to flee Nigeria, three months after the US visa was issued.29 When asked why he obtained his US visa in July 2017, three months prior to his decision to flee, if he only decided to obtain the US visa in order to flee Nigeria, the Appellant's testimony evolved significantly. He changed his testimony to indicate that right from when his problems began he needed to get a visa "in case of anything," contrary to his earlier testimony that he obtained the US visa to escape Nigeria to save his life.30 When asked why he delayed leaving Nigeria for three months after he received his US visa, the Appellant alleged that he believed he could manage the situation.31 However, this is different from what he had earlier alleged, that he applied for the US visa in July 2017 in order to flee to save his life. Indeed, despite being in possession of a valid US visitor visa, on September 18, 2017, the Appellant decided to visit to the APC chairman, his agent of persecution. Even after this visit, where he alleges that he was given a warning and a two-week deadline to join the APC, the Appellant remained in Nigeria for a further month.

Counsel argues that the RPD was microscopic in its findings on a peripheral issue. I disagree. The Appellant's evolving testimony about why he applied for a US visa and when he decided to flee Nigeria, as well as his delay in leaving Nigeria, are not peripheral concerns in the evaluation of his credibility. Rather, the Appellant's purpose for obtaining the US visa, as well as when and why he decided to flee Nigeria, go to the core of his claim that he is at risk in Nigeria.

Moreover, while not on its own determinative, the Appellant's delay in fleeing Nigeria impacts his credibility. Counsel argues that because the Appellant is married with children, was economically established in Nigeria, and was on a mission to assist his political party, it is reasonable for him to have remained in Nigeria to exhaust all avenues before fleeing.32 However, this is not the Appellant's explanation for delaying his departure from Nigeria. Contrary to Counsel's submissions, the Appellant did not provide any of these explanations at his RPD hearing when he was asked about his three-month delay. Rather, he explained that he believed he could manage the situation.33 Counsel's submission is not supported by the Record.

Having independently assessed the evidence, I find that the RPD did not err in relying on its concerns about the Appellant's evolving testimony and delay in fleeing Nigeria in its credibility analysis. I find these issues undermine the Appellant's credibility. The inconsistent PDP letter undermines the Appellant's credibility

The RPD considered the 2016 PDP letter, which states that the Appellant's XXXX was invaded on May 30, 2016.34 This is inconsistent with the Appellant's allegation that his XXXX was invaded on April 20, 2016.35 The Appellant was asked about this discrepancy at the RPD hearing and explained that he had never noticed this before and that this must be an error.36 The RPD did not find this explanation reasonable and it drew an adverse inference as to the Appellant's credibility based on his submission of this inconsistent document.

I appreciate that superficial errors should not be unreasonably focused on in assessing a document, especially as "clerical errors are possible even in countries where public administration have access to vast resources."37 However, it is not the case that this error was minor or typographical in nature. The letter refers to both the wrong month and day, despite being issued on the very same day that the PDP states that the XXXX attack took place, May 30, 2016. Counsel argues that this credibility concern has been repaired by the 2019 PDP letter, proposed as new evidence. However, as already explained above in my Reasons, this new 2019 PDP letter is inadmissible and I have not considered it in assessing the merits of the Appellant's appeal. Besides arguing that the new PDP letter corrects the earlier error, Counsel identifies no further errors in this RPD finding.

Having independently assessed the evidence, I find that the RPD did not err in relying on the inconsistent PDP letter in its credibility analysis. I find that this inconsistency is material and undermines the Appellant's credibility, including the credibility of his allegation that his XXXX was invaded, and his XXXX manager was physically attacked, as alleged, on April 20, 2016. The Appellant's supporting evidence is insufficient to outweigh credibility concerns

The Appellant provided multiple supporting documents, including business registration documents, an excerpt from his personal business book "You Can", newspaper articles regarding general political violence and herdsmen attacks in Nigeria, photographs of his XXXX manager's injuries, a medical report confirming his XXXX manager's injuries, PDP party cards, a further PDP letter corroborating his party membership, as well as three supporting sworn statements from a XXXX neighbour, a PDP party member, and the XXXX manager who was physically present during the alleged invasions of the Appellant's XXXX in April 2016 and September 2017.38 The RPD reviewed and considered all of this evidence in its Reasons within the context of the Appellant's overall credibility, correctly noting that "overall credibility may affect the weight given to the documentary evidence."39 The RPD determined that the Appellant's supporting documents are insufficient to establish his central allegations, on a balance of probabilities, and do not outweigh or overcome its credibility concerns.40 The RPD found insufficient credible evidence that members of the APC, either currently or previously, have any interest in the Appellant.41 Counsel argues that the RPD erred by failing to consider what facts are established by the supporting evidence which, when considered on a cumulative basis, establish his claim as credible. Having independently assessed the evidence, I am not persuaded by Counsel's argument. The PDP party member's affidavit and the farm neighbour's affidavit

I note that the affidavit from the PDP party member corroborates the Appellant's PDP membership, but does not purport firsthand knowledge of any of the alleged XXXX attacks and threats.42 The affidavit from the XXXX neighbor corroborates the XXXX manager's injuries and hospitalization in April 2016, but does not allege firsthand knowledge of the political nature of the attack.43 Having considered the entire Record on a cumulative basis, I find that the affidavit evidence from the neighbor and PDP member is insufficient to outweigh the multiple material credibility concerns. The XXXX manager's affidavit and supporting evidence

The XXXX manager's affidavit, photos, and medical report corroborate his physical injuries and that an assault took place on April 20, 2016.44 The affidavit also corroborates the Appellant's allegation that the XXXX was attacked in April 2016 and September 2017, and that the September 2017 attack was politically motivated. In accordance with the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Sellan, I have considered whether the XXXX manager's evidence constitutes independent and credible evidence capable of supporting the Appellant's claim, despite his own lack of credibility as a witness.45 However, this decision "does not stand for the principle that the RAD cannot make a negative credibility finding where there is independent and credible documentary evidence capable of supporting a positive determination."46 In order to determine whether the Appellant's claim succeeds based on this evidence, I have considered its credibility, probative value, weight, and sufficiency.47 I acknowledge that the photos and medical report corroborate the XXXX manager's injuries and that the affidavit, which is a sworn statement, is probative and supports the Appellant's allegations. However, it is my role to weigh the evidence before me. I recall that the Appellant submitted contradictory supporting evidence with an incorrect month and day that his XXXX was attacked.48 This evidence contradicts the XXXX manager's affidavit. This inconsistency as between the Appellant's supporting documents undermines the credibility of this alleged event. I do not find that this evidence is sufficient to outweigh the negative credibility inferences or that it supports a positive disposition of the claim.

I further acknowledge that corroborative evidence should not be disbelieved simply because a Claimant is not believed.49 However, it is open to the RPD and the RAD to analyze supporting documents within the context of a claim, including its credibility findings, as a Claimant's lack of credibility can extend to their supporting documents.50 I recall here that the Appellant lacks credibility regarding the threats that he allegedly received from the APC, as well as when he decided that his life was at risk in Nigeria and he must flee, and why he delayed leaving Nigeria for three months, even visiting an alleged agent of persecution during this period despite being in possession of a valid US visitor visa.

Having considered the entire record on a cumulative basis, I find that the XXXX manager's evidence is insufficient to outweigh the multiple material credibility concerns. The Appellant's political profile

Counsel also argues that the RPD failed to take into consideration the Appellant's alleged PDP profile. As such, I have conducted an independent assessment. The Appellant alleged in his narrative that he is a XXXX and also a "XXXX" of the PDP.51 However, in testimony he alleged that he does not make financial contributions to the party; when asked about his narrative which describes him as a financier, the Appellant explained that he XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX52 When asked how any of this relates to the PDP, the Appellant testified that "I did it for the youth" and that you can use whatever you have to bring people to the party.53

I note that the RPD did not rely on the Appellant's inconsistent evidence about whether he was or was not a party XXXX in its decision. However, credibility is the determinative issue and Counsel raised the Appellant's political profile in the memorandum, declaring that the evidence provided is "incontrovertible."54 As such, I find that this is not a new issue and it is not procedurally unfair for me to go on and, in accordance with Counsel's own submissions in the memorandum, assess the credibility of the evidence regarding the Appellant's alleged political profile.55 Moreover, the RAD is entitled to make independent credibility findings where credibility was at issue before the RPD, the RPD's findings on credibility are contested on appeal, and the RAD's additional findings arise from the evidentiary record.56 I find that the Appellant's inconsistency about whether he is a financier of the PDP or not undermines the credibility of his alleged political profile. Political violence in Nigeria and the PDP 2019 electoral results

I acknowledge that political violence occurs in Nigeria and that during elections both the PDP and APC have been accused of using violent means to intimidate opponents and attack party rallies.57 The Appellant's own party, the PDP, claimed electoral victory in Oyo state in March 2019, and the APC remains in control of other government institutions in the country.58 I acknowledge that the Appellant is a member of the PDP. However, I do not find that this establishes that his allegations of past persecution are credible, on a balance of probabilities, or that he faces a forward-looking serious possibility of persecution, or a personalized section 97(1) risk from the APC, upon return to Nigeria. The evidence adduced by the Appellant indicates that political opponents in particular leadership positions, such as a PDP chairman and an Oyo state government secretary, as well as popular musical artists, face targeting and violence.59 This is distinguishable from the Appellant's particular profile in the PDP, as a party member who provides training and his personal book for free to young people. While he may be a valuable member of the PDP who is loyal and committed, as described by the PDP, I do not find that this establishes a profile upon return to Nigeria such that he faces a serious possibility of persecution or a subsection 97 risk.60 I find that the RPD did not err.

After carefully considering all the evidence before me, I find that the Appellant is, on a balance of probabilities, not credible. Based on my own review of the Record, I find that the presumption of truthfulness has been rebutted. I have considered the Appellant's testimony and the corroboration presented, weighed against the negative credibility findings, which go to the core of his claim. I find that the Appellant has not credibly established, on a balance of probabilities, his allegations of past persecution, or that he faces a serious possibility of persecution, or a subsection 97(1) risk upon return to Nigeria. I find that the RPD did not err in its conclusion that the claim fails on the issue of credibility.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. (signed) "J. Pollock" J.
